# Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance

**Authors:** Tingli Qian; Weijin Wang; Shilong Gao; Aiko Muraishi; Beibei Zhao; Davi Nakajima An; Fanglei Xue; Max Kazman; Johnny Mendoza; Hannah Nguyen; Asim Bera; Alex Kang; Avery Yang; Wenzhao Dai; Jia Liang; Yujia Wang; Xiongyi Huang; Frank DiMaio; David Baker

Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA | 5Department of Chemistry, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA | 6Graduate Program in Biological Physics, Structure and Design, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA | 7Graduate Program in Bioengineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA | 8Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA

## Abstract

De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7Å crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.

De novo enzyme design seeks to create protein sequences that fold into stable structures while positioning catalytic functional groups and ligands with atomic precision.1–5 Recent deep-learning-based approaches address different parts of this problem, including enzyme-sequence generators such as ProtGPT2 and ZymCTRL, reaction-and-pocket-conditioned models such as EnzymeFlow and GENzyme, and structure-generative motif-scaffolding models including RFdiffusion, RFdiffusion2 (RFD2) and RFdiffusion3 (RFD3)6–20. It is not only necessary to generate protein structures that harbor the desired site, but also to identify sequences which are confidently predicted to fold to these structures; a current challenge is that as the complexity of the active site increases, it becomes more and more difficult to identify designs predicted to precisely recapitulate the site. Iterative sequence–structure optimization can improve design qualities,21,22 but current approaches provide limited ability to improve catalytic geometry. While structure prediction models have template-based backbone constraints, for enzyme active sites what is critical is the geometry of the active site and in particular the side chain–small molecule interactions, and these are not readily specified in the above methods.

Given an atomic level active site description, and candidate designs harboring the active site, we set out to develop a general method for optimizing both the structure and sequence to achieve high precision active site recapitulation. We reasoned that this optimization could be achieved by iteratively guiding structure prediction calculations toward the designed structure and the specified catalytic geometry, and then progressively removing this guidance, analogous to teacher-policy annealing in reinforcement-learning in which expert supervision supports early learning and is progressively withdrawn as training proceeds.23,24 Whereas text-to-image diffusion models commonly use inference-time guidance scales greater than 1 to strengthen conditioning,25,26 we reasoned that such constraint fading could be achieved by decreasing inference guidance below 1 across design cycles. We set out to explore this approach which we call CaGE– catalytic guidance engine for de novo design of enzymes with complex active sites.

## Results

Figure 1 outlines the basic idea underlying our approach. While a design model may place catalytic residues and ligands in the intended geometry, structure predictions based on the designed sequence often fail to recover this arrangement (Fig. 1a). This problem is typically overcome by generating large numbers of designs and filtering for those with predicted structures satisfying the input constraints, but for complex constraint sets the fraction of such internally consistent design can be extremely low, making this approach computationally prohibitive. To bring structure predictions closer to the designed geometry, we began with the RosettaFold3 (RF3)27 structure prediction method, trained it with design conditions and incorporated guidance. Incorporation of suitably weighted design based active site conditioning as expected brings the generated models to the designed structure (Fig. 1b,c).

However, structure–sequence agreement under guidance does not ensure that the sequence will recover the site when this guidance is removed. To overcome this problem, we turned to classifier free guidance,25 which combines conditional and unconditional denoising directions at adjustable scales (see below and Methods). Whereas inference-time guidance in image-generation diffusion models commonly uses scales greater than 1 to strengthen conditioning, we reasoned that iterative guidance with scales lower than 1 could be used to progressively withdraw guidance over successive design cycles to arrive at designed sequences which encode the designed sites. (Fig. 1d).

### Incorporation of constraint conditioning in RF3

CAGE requires the ability to condition a structure prediction method on constraint sets similar to those used in design calculations. While structure prediction methods such as AF3 or Boltz,28,29 allow template-based backbone constraints, for enzyme active sites what is critical is the geometry of the active site and in particular the side chain–small molecule interactions, and these are not readily specified in the above methods.

We extended RF3 training to incorporate additional design conditions. RF3 has an overall AF3-like architecture, with a pairformer trunk feeding a diffusion module that generates all-atom coordinates. We extended its training to incorporate five types of design condition: interface hotspots, relative solvent accessibility, hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor identities, interface type, and atom-pair distances (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 1). Interface hotspots inform target binding sites (Supplementary Figure 2), whereas relative solvent accessibility specifies the desired exposure or burial of selected atoms to water. Hydrogen-bond conditions identify atoms intended to act as donors or acceptors, and interface-type conditioning specifies the class of molecular interface, such as a protein–DNA interface. Atom-pair distance conditioning specifies the identities of two atoms and their target separation without imposing an absolute coordinate frame.

### Classifier-free guidance combines and adjusts the strength of design conditions

With these design conditions learned by the structure prediction model, we controlled the relative influence of the different design conditions on the final structure output with classifier-free guidance. Using CFG, multiple design conditions can be combined at independently adjustable strengths, allowing their contributions to be independently and progressively reduced across design cycles. For each condition i, the CFG scale αᵢ interpolates between the unconditional prediction (αᵢ = 0) and the conditional prediction (αᵢ = 1): setting αᵢ = 0 removes its contribution entirely, whereas αᵢ = 1 retains it at full strength.

For enzyme design, we combined atom-pair distance conditioning with template-based conditioning to guide backbone geometry and ligand placement towards the target theozyme configuration, including catalytic side-chain geometry at atomic resolution5. We selected eight enzyme targets spanning diverse catalytic motifs and ligand environments to evaluate whether CaGE could accommodate different geometric constraints on catalytic residues and ligand placement. These comprised purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP), ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), 4-chlorobenzoyl-CoA dehalogenase (4-CBA-CoA DH), enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase) and citrate synthase (CS) (Fig. 2a), together with UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GalE), glycosidase (GLY) and UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase (UGDH) (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Increasing the classifier-free guidance scale α for atom-pair distance conditioning from 0 to 1 reduced the median motif r.m.s.d. across the tested targets (Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure 4a). At matched CFG scales, RF3 trained with atom-pair distance conditioning achieved lower median motif r.m.s.d. than RF3 without this conditioning (Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure 4a).

### Motif guidance enables precise geometric control without additional training

Training can incorporate a broad range of design conditions, enabling control over diverse molecular properties. To enable utilization of a broader range of structure prediction models, we also developed a training-free alternative for geometric control termed motif guidance. At each denoising step, motif guidance corrects the clean estimate x ^ 0 , thereby steering the diffusion trajectory toward the designed geometry, with μ adjusting the strength of the correction.

Without atom-pair distance-conditioning, increasing motif guidance strength μ from 0 to 1 while holding CFG at its maximum tested scale (α = 1) further reduced motif r.m.s.d. across targets relative to CFG alone (Fig. 2a). On our enzyme-design benchmarks, motif guidance combined with CFG achieved motif accuracy comparable to that obtained with atom-pair distance-conditioning training and CFG. Representative structural comparisons across all targets illustrate progressive improvements in catalytic-motif geometry with increasing guidance strength (Supplementary Fig. 3).

### Guided and unguided predictions converge across cycles

To test the mechanism proposed in Fig. 1d, in which successive rounds of structure prediction and sequence redesign reduce reliance on external guidance as sequences become more compatible with the target active-site geometry, we compared guided predictions with independent unguided refolds of identical amino acid sequences within each cycle. This comparison assessed whether the target active-site geometry could increasingly be recovered without external guidance during iterative prediction and sequence redesign. As guidance progressively decreased, the difference between median joint motif–ligand r.m.s.d. values narrowed monotonically across all eight targets (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 4b). This convergence supports the proposed transition from guidance-dependent geometry towards geometry that is increasingly supported by the redesigned sequences.

### CaGE recovers active-site geometry in unguided RF3 and AF3 predictions

We next evaluated CaGE across eight enzyme targets, using sequences designed on RFD3-generated backbones without CaGE cycling as the baseline. The final CaGE cycle was completed without guidance, and the final sequences were subsequently evaluated with AF3. Across the five targets shown in Fig. 2, CaGE AF3 predictions had lower median motif and ligand r.m.s.d. values than baseline predictions (Fig. 2c).

We assessed two joint pass criteria: motif r.m.s.d. <1.25 Å and ligand r.m.s.d. <5 Å (strict), or motif r.m.s.d. ≤1.5 Å and ligand r.m.s.d. ≤5 Å (relaxed). Fig. 2d shows the sequence-level pass rate: the percentage of evaluated designed sequences meeting each joint criterion. For the five targets shown in Fig. 2, CaGE increased this pass rate at both motif thresholds. At the 1.5-Å motif r.m.s.d. threshold, CaGE increased pass rates across targets. More notably, at the more stringent 1.25-Å threshold, CaGE recovered passing designs for challenging targets where the baseline yielded none, achieving pass rates of 8.11%, 1.57% and 0.32% for PNP, ODC and 4-CBA-CoA DH, respectively (Fig. 2d). After normalizing with the number of structure-prediction calls for efficiency analysis, CaGE produced more passing sequences per 1,000 prediction calls than the RFD3 baseline for all five targets at both motif cutoffs (Fig. 2e). Among designs passing the 1.5-Å motif criterion, CaGE designs occupied structure clusters not represented among the sampled baseline successes (Supplementary Fig. 5).

At the 1.25-Å motif cutoff, this yield increased from 0.62 to 8.06 for crotonase and from 1.25 to 2.46 for CS. The baseline yielded no passing sequences for PNP, ODC or 4-CBA-CoA DH at this cutoff, whereas CaGE yielded 5.579, 4.889 and 1.078 per 1,000 structure prediction calls, respectively. The advantage persisted for all five targets when the motif cutoff was relaxed to 1.5 Å. Results for the three additional targets, GalE, GLY and UGDH, are reported in Supplementary Fig. 4d,e. Representative AF3 predictions illustrate the recovered catalytic-motif geometries and ligand poses relative to the target theozymes (Fig. 2f).

### CaGE refines a coupled nonheme-iron catalytic motif

To test whether CaGE could recover coupled metal-coordination and reaction-state geometry, we designed scaffolds around a nonheme-iron transition-state motif for a C–N bond-forming rearrangement (Fig. 3a). The motif comprises a mononuclear iron centre, its first-shell coordinating residues and a transition-state ligand spanning the reacting fragments, requiring simultaneous recovery of the coordination sphere and reactive geometry. This motif is challenging to scaffold and recover in structure prediction because it combines a non-native transition-state ligand with multiple coupled degrees of freedom governing metal coordination and the relative positioning of the reacting fragments.

We compared unoptimised RFdiffusion3–LigandMPNN30 designs with sequences generated after one CaGE cycle, starting from the same pool of 1,500 backbones sampled before additional filtering or refinement. Following identical sequence-quality filtering, 1,491 baseline sequences and 1,701 CaGE sequences were evaluated using the same unguided AF3 protocol, with five diffusion samples per sequence. One CaGE cycle increased the fraction meeting a catalytic-motif r.m.s.d. threshold of 1.25 Å from 0.27% to 4.70%, and a threshold of 1.5 Å from 0.80% to 10.29%, with both criteria additionally requiring ligand r.m.s.d. ≤ 5 Å (Fig. 3b). These rates measure recovery per evaluated sequence and exclude backbones discarded during cycling. The broader structural distributions also shifted toward the target geometry: median Fe-triad distance deviation decreased from 8.80 to 1.81 Å, and median ligand r.m.s.d. decreased from 11.40 to 5.39 Å (Fig. 3c). Thus, one CaGE cycle generated sequences whose unguided predictions better recovered both metal coordination and ligand placement.

We next scaled up the CaGE calculations to generate designs to experimentally test. We applied four CaGE refinement cycles, with the CFG scale reduced from 1.0 to zero. Final unguided AF3 evaluation identified 160 designs that satisfied the fold and complete motif criteria in at least three of five diffusion samples. Of 71 designs screened experimentally, six produced product signals above the no-enzyme control. The design CaGE-13M showed activity and yielded products with 83% enantiomeric excess (Fig. 3d). This result supports involvement of the designed active site in controlling the reaction outcome. Together, these results connect improved computational recovery of a coupled catalytic motif with experimental activity and stereoselectivity in a designed nonheme-iron scaffold.

CaGE-13M is a 209-residue protein with a mononuclear iron site coordinated by His39, His147 and Asp43, with Asn187 also positioned in the active site (Fig. 3e). An independent AF3 prediction recovered the backbone and catalytic residues with r.m.s.d. values of 1.00 and 1.02 Å, respectively, and a ligand distance deviation of 0.80 Å.

### De novo design and experimental validation of a PLP-dependent retro-aldolase

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is a versatile biological cofactor that supports diverse transformations, including transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, carbon–carbon bond cleavage and formation, and β- and γ-elimination reactions.31 Its reactivity arises from formation of a Schiff base with a catalytic lysine or amino-group-containing substrate, allowing the conjugated pyridinium system to stabilize high-energy carbanionic intermediates.

PLP-dependent catalysis therefore provides a stringent test for de novo enzyme design. Productive catalysis requires the protein to position a catalytic lysine for internal-aldimine formation, recognize the PLP phosphate, tune the electronic state of the pyridine ring, orient the substrate relative to the cofactor and stabilize multiple intermediates along the reaction coordinate. These requirements go substantially beyond simple cofactor binding. To our knowledge, no PLP-dependent enzyme has previously been generated by de novo scaffolding of a predefined PLP catalytic motif.

We therefore applied CaGE to the design of a PLP-dependent retro-aldolase that cleaves a β-hydroxy amino acid into the corresponding aldehyde and glycine through a PLP external aldimine (Fig. 4a). The catalytic motif contained four residues surrounding the PLP–substrate complex (Fig. 4b). Lys142 was positioned to form the resting-state PLP internal aldimine, Asp27 to interact with the PLP pyridine nitrogen, His31 to form a π interaction with the PLP pyridine ring and contact the substrate β-hydroxyl group, and Arg159 to recognize and orient the substrate carboxylate. Together, these interactions defined an atomically specified catalytic arrangement coupling cofactor activation with substrate positioning.

Starting from this motif, candidate scaffolds were generated using RFdiffusion3, LigandMPNN and iterative FastRelax32–LigandMPNN refinement before CaGE cycling. None of the 30,293 pre-CaGE sequences passed the final AF3 geometric criteria when evaluated under the same protocol used for the CaGE candidates. CaGE refinement yielded 1,029 variants passing the final unguided RF3 filters, of which 96 also passed independent AF3 validation without a protein template or supplied ligand pose.

A lysate-based primary screen of the 96 computationally selected first-round designs identified CaGE-RA1.0 as an active hit (Supplementary Fig. 7). Primary screening was performed with 2.5 mM β-hydroxy amino-acid substrate and 25 μM PLP in 100 mM potassium phosphate (KPi), pH 8.0, at 30 °C for 16 h. CaGE-RA1.0 was subsequently expressed at larger scale, purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography, and its activity was confirmed using purified protein under matched reaction conditions. Its AF3 prediction closely reproduced the design model, with PLP–substrate ligand r.m.s.d. value of 1.30 Å, respectively (Fig. 4c). Thus, the designed geometry was independently recovered from sequence rather than maintained only by structural guidance.

CaGE-RA1.0 was designed as a compact monomer, with the PLP-binding and catalytic environment contained within a single polypeptide chain. This architecture differs from canonical natural PLP-dependent threonine aldolases,33 which typically adopt evolved PLP-enzyme folds relying on oligomeric assemblies. CaGE-RA1.0 therefore represents a structurally distinct solution in which PLP-dependent carbon–carbon bond chemistry is embedded within a de novo monomeric scaffold.

### Hit-guided redesign improves catalytic activity

We next asked whether an experimentally validated first-round hit could provide a starting point for further CaGE optimization. CaGE-RA1.0 was used as the structural template for a second design round while retaining the catalytic motif (Fig. 4c). Rather than sampling mutations independently, the redesign allowed coordinated sequence and structural changes around the active site while preserving the validated global architecture. The resulting design, CaGE-RA1.1, again showed close agreement between the design model and AF3 prediction, with ligand r.m.s.d. value of 0.94 Å, respectively (Fig. 4c). This redesign also improved catalytic performance. Under matched conditions, CaGE-RA1.0 produced 22.8 ± 1.6% product, whereas CaGE-RA1.1 reached 41.4 ± 1.7% yield (mean ± s.d., n = 3 independent reactions), corresponding to an approximately 1.8-fold improvement (Fig. 4d). Thus, the same framework used to generate the initial active scaffold could subsequently improve an experimentally validated hit without a large combinatorial mutagenesis campaign.

### Mechanistic and structural validation of the designed PLP enzyme

To test whether activity depended on the intended catalytic architecture, each of the four designed catalytic residues in CaGE-RA1.0 was individually replaced with alanine (Fig. 4e). D27A, H31A, K142A and R159A all reduced product formation to approximately the no-protein background, indicating that activity depends on the designed residue network rather than nonspecific PLP-mediated chemistry. The strong effect of K142A is consistent with its proposed role as the covalent anchor for the resting-state PLP internal aldimine. The effects of D27A, H31A and R159A further support the importance of PLP activation and substrate positioning. Thus, residues specified geometrically during computational design were also required experimentally for productive catalysis.

We next examined the chemical state of PLP associated with CaGE-RA1.0. UV–visible spectra were recorded for 50 μM purified CaGE-RA1.0 before and after addition of one molar equivalent of PLP (50 μM) in 100 mM KPi, pH 8.0. The CaGE-RA1.0–PLP sample showed a distinct absorption profile compared with free PLP in solution (Fig. 4f), consistent with incorporation of the cofactor into a different electronic environment. Treatment of the CaGE-RA1.0–PLP complex with NaBH4 strongly diminished the visible PLP absorption feature, as expected upon reduction of a protein-bound Schiff base. We therefore used NaBH4 to trap the proposed Lys142–PLP internal aldimine and analysed the resulting protein by intact mass spectrometry (Fig. 4g). CaGE-RA1.0 showed a major apo species at 21,504 Da and an additional species at 21,735 Da following PLP loading and reductive trapping. The 231-Da mass increase is consistent with incorporation of a single PLP molecule through Schiff-base formation followed by reduction. Together with the spectroscopic measurements, these data support formation of the designed covalent PLP–lysine species rather than simple non-covalent cofactor association.

Finally, we determined the crystal structure of CaGE-RA1.0 at 2.7 Å resolution (Fig. 4h). The experimental structure closely reproduced the computational model, with a backbone r.m.s.d. of 0.702 Å, confirming that the designed global architecture was encoded by the sequence and realized experimentally. CaGE-RA1.0 also retained the intended monomeric architecture in the crystal structure. This distinguishes the design from canonical PLP-dependent threonine aldolases, in which oligomerization is a common structural feature, and demonstrates that the requirements for PLP-dependent carbon–carbon bond cleavage can be accommodated within a compact single-chain scaffold.

## Discussion

Here, we introduce CaGE, an iterative enzyme-design framework that combines guided structure prediction with sequence redesign and progressively withdraws the guidance to obtain sequences which encode structures satisfying complex sets of constraints. Sequence design methods such as ProteinMPNN find sequences which maximize P(sequence| structure), but the maximum of P(structure|sequence) for these sequences may not be the designed structure; CaGE effectively nudges the designed sequence towards encoding the designed structure. CaGE uses model forward passes rather than backpropagation and so is considerably faster than hallucination approaches which also optimize sequences to encode desired structures34,35. Protein Hunter and HalluDesign have shown the effectiveness of iterative prediction-and-redesign cycles for binder design, where protein-protein interactions can be viewed as an inherently known design condition in structure prediction models. CaGE goes considerably beyond these approaches by incorporating a broad range of conditioning information on atom-pair distance distances and other protein properties relevant to enzymatic and other functions, and gradually fading this information during design iterations to nudge the designed sequence to accurately encode the designed constraints. The wide range of conditioning gives CaGE broad versatility, for example, hotspot conditioning could direct antibody binding to selected hotspots on an antigen, interface-type conditioning could specify the class of binding partner for design of multicomponent protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and RASA conditioning could guide ligand and pH-dependent binding proteins.

Our experimental tests show that CaGE can yield functional designs under different catalytic constraints. In the nonheme-iron system, CaGE-13M produced a product signal above background with 83% enantiomeric excess, whereas the no-enzyme and coordination-site-mutant controls were racemic. The PLP-dependent retro-aldolase has a crystal structure nearly identical to the design model, substitutions at the four designed catalytic positions reduce product formation to near background, and spectroscopy and reductive trapping support formation of the intended protein–PLP Schiff-base species. CaGE refinement increased the endpoint product yield, illustrating a further use of the workflow in improving an experimentally identified hit.

CaGE illustrates how a structure predictor can act as a design engine, guiding iterative changes to sequences and structures toward a prescribed catalytic geometry. Our inference-time guidance strategies enable use of multiple off the shelf prediction methods in CaGE, and could further improve performance by avoiding possible biases associated with a single method. More broadly, CaGE shows how learned sequence–structure relationships can support both prediction and controlled molecular design, suggesting a foundation for biological world models that predict the consequences of molecular changes and guide interventions toward desired functions.
